S062.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
S062.description: Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation that is out of proportion to the actual danger. (Note: In children, may be expressed by crying, tantrums, freezing, or clinging).

subtypes.Animal Type: Marked fear of animals or insects like dogs, bees, snakes, or spiders.
subtypes.Natural Environment Type: Marked fear of the natural environment like storms, heights, water, or the dark.
subtypes.Blood-Injection-Injury Type: Marked fear of seeing blood, receiving injections, or medical procedures.
subtypes.Situational Type: Marked fear of specific situations like airplanes, elevators, tunnels, bridges, or enclosed spaces.
subtypes.Other Type: Marked fear of other situations like choking, vomiting, loud sounds, or costumed characters.

S063.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
S063.description: The phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety.

subtypes.Anticipatory Anxiety: Strong anxiety triggered just by thinking about the possibility of encountering the phobic object.
subtypes.Immediate Panic Response: Overwhelming fear erupting immediately upon facing the phobic object.
subtypes.Physiological Panic Symptoms: Intense physical reactions such as heart palpitations, shortness of breath, sweating, or trembling.
subtypes.Freezing: Feeling paralyzed or unable to move due to extreme fear.

S064.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
S064.description: The phobic object or situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety.

subtypes.Active Avoidance: Intentionally and completely staying away from contact with the phobic object or situation.
subtypes.Functional Impairment due to Avoidance: Accepting severe restrictions on daily life, job, or social activities to avoid the phobic object.
subtypes.Enduring with Distress: Forcing oneself to endure the situation while experiencing intense fear and anxiety because it cannot be avoided.
subtypes.Reliance on Safety Signals: Barely enduring the exposure by relying on a companion or safety object.

symptom.disease_info: Specific Phobia is characterized by a marked, persistent fear of a clearly identifiable object or situation that is excessive or out of proportion to the actual risk, and that consistently provokes intense anxiety and avoidance. The feared stimulus is either actively avoided or endured with significant distress, and this pattern must last at least six months and cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Onset often follows a discrete frightening or painful event involving the stimulus, vicarious learning (e.g., witnessing others’ fear), or informational transmission, and the course tends to be chronic if untreated, with individuals often organizing their lives to minimize contact with the phobic trigger. It is distinguished from other anxiety disorders by the narrow, circumscribed nature of the fear and the absence of broader, unexpected panic attacks or pervasive worry about multiple domains.

patient.personality: Jeffery is a hyper-organized, competitive young auditor who channels his restless energy into precision, efficiency, and constant self-optimization in both work and leisure.
patient.stressor: Just over two years ago, during a weekend hike in the Texas Hill Country with coworkers, Jeffery was bitten by a large dog that broke free from its owner on a narrow trail, knocking him down and leaving him briefly pinned and convinced he would lose control of the situation. Although the physical wounds healed quickly and the dog’s vaccinations were up to date, the event clashed sharply with his usual sense of control and meticulous planning, leaving a strong emotional imprint. Over time he began subtly reorganizing his routines—changing running routes, declining friends’ invitations to outdoor events, and even avoiding clients’ offices where he knew dogs were present—until these workarounds grew so extensive that he was turning down engagements and skipping runs he once treated as non-negotiable. When he realized he was spending significant time and mental energy plotting how to avoid any chance encounters with dogs, and it started to interfere with both his job opportunities and his main coping outlet of distance running, he decided to seek psychiatric evaluation at the urging of a mentor who noticed his growing rigidity.
patient.chief_complaint: “I have this intense, irrational fear whenever I might run into a dog, and it’s starting to control where I go and what I do.”

S062.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
S062.description: Marked fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation that is out of proportion to the actual danger. (Note: In children, may be expressed by crying, tantrums, freezing, or clinging).
S062.manifestation: Ever since that hike, any time I even see a dog in the distance—on a leash, behind a fence, whatever—my brain jumps straight to, ‘it’s going to break loose and come after me,’ and the fear feels way bigger than what’s actually in front of me, but I can’t talk myself out of it in the moment.

S063.name: Immediate_Fear/Anxiety_Response
S063.description: The phobic object or situation almost always provokes immediate fear or anxiety.
S063.manifestation: If I turn a corner on the sidewalk and suddenly there’s a dog there, my heart slams into overdrive, my hands start shaking, and it’s like my whole body locks up for a second before I can back away, even if the dog is tiny and the owner’s apologizing that it’s friendly.

S064.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
S064.description: The phobic object or situation is actively avoided or endured with intense fear or anxiety.
S064.manifestation: I plan my runs, my commute, even which clients I’ll visit around where dogs might be, and if I can’t avoid a situation—like walking up to a house with a ‘beware of dog’ sign—I’ll only do it if someone comes with me and I’m still gripping the railing or my bag the whole time, just counting the seconds until I can get away.
